blocks.text: VII. He (in the Sacred Miscellanies, book 6, ch. 11) understands both by דביונים and by חריונים (the former is written in the margin, the latter in the text) the crop of doves, [II, 578] their belly and entrails. It is as if they were called דביונים, that is, the flux of doves, because those who cut up and gut doves let these flow down, or slip, to the ground; and חריונים, that is, κοιλία [koilia], or the belly of doves. For he tries to prove that חריונים are the belly and entrails of doves as follows: "The Hebrew חור first "means white; 2. a hole, from the brightness of the light that is usually seen through it; 3. "τρώγλην [trōglēn], a cavity, which is a kind of hole; 4. the belly, in Greek κοιλίαν [koilian], "which is the chief cavity of the human body; whence alvus [belly] is named as if alveus [hollow], and κοιλία [koilia] "from κοῖλον [koilon]; 5. the excrement enclosed in the belly, by a metonymy of the content "for the container. Since we may choose the most "suitable of these meanings of the word, why should we not take it here to mean the belly and entrails of doves, which, "though usually thrown away, in a time of most severe famine were not only kept, "but were even sold off and disposed of at a high price." This is the opinion of Fuller, in which (if I may say so with the leave of a most careful writer) I seem to have found a good many things that have not even the appearance of truth. Thus, that the entrails of doves should be called דביונים in Hebrew never occurred to anyone even in a dream. Rather, all explain it as dung, so called from flowing, just as in Greek ῥεῦμα γαστρὸς [rheuma gastros] and διάῤῥοια [diarrhoia], and in Latin alvi profluvium [flux of the belly], are said of such a flux. And in Celsus febres fluentes [flowing fevers], in Greek ῥοώδεις πυρετοὶ [rhoōdeis pyretoi], are those that loosen the bowels. Again, in what the same Fuller asserts, that the word חור means 1. white, 2. a hole, 3. a cavity, 4. the belly, crop, entrails, 5. dung, most of it is invented. חור for white is not so much Hebrew as Chaldee and Arabic. But for a hole or a cavity it is Hebrew, and from a different root. For the former is from חור chavar, to grow white; the latter from the geminate חרר charar, to perforate. Accordingly in the Talmud, tractate Succa, fol. 20b, you may read חור שחררוהו מים, a hole which the waters have bored. And for the same Talmudists חריר is the eye of a needle, as ܚܪܘܪܐ is for the Syrians in Matth. XIX, 24. Further, that this חור also means belly, or crop, or entrails [col. 43] is a pure invention, for which no authority is cited, nor indeed can be, since no one has ever used it so. Finally, חר, or rather חרי or חרא, for dung is an entirely different word, whose root is neither חור nor חרר, but חרה or חרא. Hence the Talmudists consistently write חרי or חריא. And in Arabic خري [khriy] charia, with hamza at the end, is to void excrement, خرء [khurʾ] is dung, مخرأة [makhraʾa] a latrine. Indeed the Hebrews too, when they write plene, insert an Aleph, as in Esa. XXXVI, 12. לאכול את חראיהם, to eat their own dung. And 2 Reg. X, 27. They destroyed the house of Baal and made it למחראות, into latrines. Nor is the Aleph there adventitious, as they think, but radical, and to be supplied where it is missing, as is clear from Arabic usage. With these observations made, it is evident that the distinguished Fuller did not know the etymology of the word or its true spelling, and indiscriminately took three words of different origin, which led him astray. For since everything he adduces rests solely [II, 579] on the etymologies of words, if these etymologies are false, whatever is built upon them must also be false. And indeed it is most frivolous, what he attributes to the sacred author, that a cab of the bellies and entrails of doves sold at Samaria for five shekels. For it has never been heard tell that the crop and entrails of doves were sold separately. I admit that I have read this of hens, and that in Arabic تبودك [tbwdk] thabudach is said of one who sells the entrails of a hen, namely the heart, crop, etc. Alcamus explains it as من يبيع ما في بطون الدجاج من القلب والقانصة [man yabīʿu mā fī buṭūn al-dajāj min al-qalb wa-l-qāniṣa]. But of those of doves nothing of the kind occurs anywhere, so far as I know. Nor is it fitting that the intestines of doves should have been measured by cabs. For the cab is a measure not of entrails but of grain, like the seah, the ephah and the cor. Namely, six cabs make a seah, three seahs an ephah, ten ephahs a cor, the largest dry measure. Accordingly in the Talmud and in the Aruch you may read everywhere קב חטין, a cab of wheat. And it is defined by Elias as מדת היובש, a measure of dry things; by Pomarius as מדת של חטים, a measure of grain; by Aquinas as מדת למדות דבר היבש, a measure for measuring a dry thing. So in Pollux: Κάβασον δὲ ἐκάλουν τὸν περὶ τὴν τροφὴν ἄπληστον, etc. Κάβος γὰρ σίτου μέτρον. [Kabason de ekaloun ton peri tēn trophēn aplēston, etc. Kabos gar sitou metron.] And they called a man insatiable for food a cabasus, etc. For the cab is a measure of grain. And in Hesychius: Κάβαισος· ἄπληστος· κάβος γὰρ μέτρον σιτικόν· [Kabaisos; aplēstos; kabos gar metron sitikon;] Cabasus, insatiable; for the cab is a measure of grain. From this correct Suidas, who has κάβαιστος [kabaistos] for κάβαισος [kabaisos]; and the Etymologicon, which has μετασιτικὸν [metasitikon], a word of no meaning, for μέτρον σιτικὸν [metron sitikon]. But in Hesychius what follows a little below is corrupt: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ οἰνικὸν [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai oinikon], Cab, a measure of grain and of wine. For that the cab is a measure of wine, or of liquids, you will read nowhere else. So I emend thus: Κάβος· μέτρον σιτικὸν, καὶ κάδος οἰνικόν· [Kabos; metron sitikon, kai kados oinikon;] The cab is a measure of grain, and the cadus of wine. He compares two words close to each other in sound as well as in meaning. For both mean a measure, but the latter of wine, the former of grain. Indeed, that the cab is a measure of grain, as the cadus is of wine, there is no one who does not know. Thus Herodotus, book 3, chapter 20, says Φοινικηΐου οἴνου κάδον [Phoinikēiou oinou kadon], a cadus of palm wine. And in book 11 of Athenaeus, Anacreon:
